This book is the story of that spacesuit. Book Review: Spacesuit: Fashioning Apollo by Nicholas de Monchaux

Review by Ron Cowen
By Science News
March 11, 2011 at 11:03 am - More than 2 years ago

Share this:

* Share
Buy this book
When Neil Armstrong took his first steps on the moon in July 1969, he wore a spacesuit fashioned by Playtex, the bra and girdle company. Playtex seamstresses assembled all the Apollo suits from 21 layers of flexible fabric, latex and reinforcements — a design that won out over the armorlike suits of interlocking components that military-industrial contractors were offering.
In 21 chapters, one for each layer, de Monchaux, an architecture professor at the University of California, Berkeley, makes the case that spacesuit design reflected changing ideas at the time about architecture, fashion and popular culture.

Many of the chapters meander from the spacesuit’s story, but the pace picks up when de Monchaux focuses on Playtex’s struggle to convince NASA to accept its softer, nontraditional design. Other companies in the late 1950s had taken a different tack — proposing to modify the human body to allow for space exploration. But “again and again, the human body resisted such encroachments,” the author contends.
Each Apollo suit was custom-fitted, so every alteration required a new fitting.

Spacesuit: Fashioning Apollo reconstructs the unlikely story of how a lingerie manufacturer — not a military contractor — put humans on the moon, reading the Apollo spacesuit as a twenty-one-layer argument about the limits of systems thinking and the intelligence of soft, adaptive complexity.

About This Book

When Neil Armstrong stepped onto the lunar surface, he was wearing a garment made by Playtex seamstresses who ordinarily stitched bras and girdles. Nicholas de Monchaux's account of that fact is far more than an amusing footnote to space history. Structured in twenty-one chapters — one for each layer of the suit — the book moves across eighteenth-century androids, Christian Dior's New Look, cybernetics, the CBS lunar broadcast soundstage, and the politics of NASA's Mission Control to argue a single, urgent thesis: that redundancy, interdependence, and adaptive complexity outperformed the hard-shell engineering logic of the military-industrial complex.
